questions.q: A budgeting app asks for your bank password so it can read your transactions. Which problem does OAuth solve here?
questions.explain: With the password, the app can do everything you can, forever, and a breach of the app is a breach of your bank. A scoped token limits the damage and can be revoked on its own.
options: It encrypts the password before the app stores it
The app gets a limited, revocable token for just the access you approved, and never sees your password
It makes the app log in faster
It lets the app share the password with other apps safely

questions.q: What does OpenID Connect add to OAuth 2.0?
questions.explain: OAuth answers "what may this app do?". OIDC answers "who just logged in?" with a standard, verifiable token and standard claims such as sub and email.
options: A signed ID token that tells the client who the user is: authentication on top of OAuth's authorization
Support for passwords in the token request

questions.q: In "Budget App reads Ada's transactions from the bank's API", which role is the bank's API?
questions.explain: Ada is the resource owner, Budget App is the client, the bank's log-in service is the authorization server, and the API that serves the data and checks tokens is the resource server.

questions.q: Why can't a single-page app or a mobile app keep a client secret?
questions.explain: These are public clients. PKCE is what protects their codes, which is why it is required for them, and recommended for confidential clients too.
options: Its code runs on users' devices, where anyone can read it, so any "secret" in it is public

questions.q: Why does the flow send a short-lived code through the browser instead of the access token itself?
questions.explain: The front channel (the browser) is exposed; the back channel (server to server) is not. The code is the minimum that must cross the front channel, and it is single-use and quick to expire.
options: Codes are shorter, so URLs stay readable
URLs leak (history, logs, Referer); a code alone is useless without the PKCE verifier (and client secret), while tokens travel only server to server
The access token is not ready until the user logs out

questions.q: What exactly is sent where in PKCE S256?
questions.explain: The hash can travel through the browser because it cannot be reversed. At the exchange, the server hashes the verifier and compares it with the challenge stored with the code.
options: The verifier in the authorization URL; the challenge at the token exchange
The challenge (SHA-256 of the verifier, base64url) in the authorization URL; the verifier itself at the token exchange
The verifier in a cookie; the challenge in the ID token

questions.q: Why should servers refuse code_challenge_method=plain?
questions.explain: PKCE's protection comes from the hash. Without it, a leaked URL gives an attacker both the code's challenge and the secret it was meant to hide. The OAuth 2.1 draft requires S256.
options: With plain, the challenge equals the verifier, so anyone who sees the authorization URL also has the verifier
It only works with confidential clients
It produces challenges that are too long

questions.q: What attack does the state parameter stop?
questions.explain: The state ties the callback to a log-in this browser started. An attacker's callback carries the attacker's state, which does not match the victim's stored one.
options: Login CSRF: an attacker making the victim's browser complete a log-in with the attacker's code

questions.q: Where should the client keep the expected state (and the PKCE verifier and nonce) between the two steps?
questions.explain: If the expected value also comes from the browser, an attacker who can set cookies controls both sides of the comparison. Server-side storage keeps the expected value out of their reach.
options: In a cookie holding the plain state, compared with the state in the callback
On the client's server, keyed by a random id in an HttpOnly cookie, deleted after one use

questions.q: What does the OIDC nonce protect against?
questions.explain: The client sends a fresh random nonce in the authorization request, and the provider copies it into the ID token. A token from any other log-in has a different nonce.
options: Replaying an ID token from another log-in: the token must carry the random nonce this log-in sent

questions.q: A client registered https://budget.example/callback. The authorization server accepts any redirect URI that starts with it. What can an attacker do?
questions.explain: Prefix and wildcard matching have led to real code leaks. Compare the whole string against the registered list, exactly.
options: Nothing; the prefix check is enough
Request codes for URIs like https://budget.example/callbackevil or ones with path tricks, and have codes delivered where they can read them

questions.q: The authorization request has an unregistered redirect_uri. What should the server do?
questions.explain: Redirecting to an unverified URI, even with an error, turns the server into an open redirect. Only verified redirect URIs ever receive a redirect.
options: Show an error on its own page, without redirecting anywhere
Redirect to the first registered URI with a code

questions.q: An authorization code that was already exchanged is presented again. What should the authorization server do?
questions.explain: Codes are single-use. A second redemption means the code exists in two places, so the tokens from the first redemption may be in the wrong hands too.
options: Issue new tokens, since the client proved PKCE
Refuse it and revoke the tokens already issued from that code
Ask the user to consent again

questions.q: Which set of checks must a client apply to an ID token?
questions.explain: Each check stops a different attack: forgery, tokens from another issuer, tokens for another app, old tokens, and tokens from another log-in.
options: Check that it has three parts
Signature with the provider's key (from its JWKS), iss is the provider, aud is this client, not expired, nonce matches
Send it to the resource server and see if it works

questions.q: An app logs users in by calling the provider's profile endpoint with whatever access token it receives. What is the flaw?
questions.explain: Access tokens do not say which client they were meant for. The ID token's aud does, which is why log-in must rely on a verified ID token (or on running the code flow yourself).
options: An access token issued to another app for the same user also works, so another app can log in to yours as that user
Access tokens cannot be sent to profile endpoints
There is no flaw if HTTPS is used

questions.q: How should the client identify the local account for an OIDC user?
questions.explain: sub is the provider's permanent, unique id for the user; combined with iss it is unique across providers. E-mails change, get recycled, and are not always verified.
options: By the issuer plus the sub claim

questions.q: A token has scope transactions:read and calls POST /api/transfers, which needs transactions:write. What should the resource server answer?
questions.explain: 401 means the token is missing, invalid or expired. A valid token without the needed scope gets 403, and the header tells the client which scope it lacks.

questions.q: Why does the OAuth 2.1 draft remove the implicit flow (response_type=token)?
questions.explain: Single-page apps once used it because they could not do a code exchange. With PKCE they can, so the code flow replaces it everywhere.
options: It returned access tokens in the URL, exposed to history, extensions and logs, with no way to bind them to the client
It was too slow for mobile apps

questions.q: A client caches the provider's JWKS. An ID token arrives with a kid that is not in the cache. What should it do?
questions.explain: Providers rotate signing keys. Refreshing on an unknown kid handles rotation; limiting how often keeps an attacker from forcing constant refetches. A key supplied by the token itself proves nothing.
options: Reject every token from now on
Skip the signature check for this token
Fetch the JWKS again (rate-limited), since the provider may have rotated keys, and reject the token if the key is still unknown
Use the first key in the cache
Trust the key embedded in the token header

questions.explain: This is the example pair from RFC 7636. The digest is encoded as base64url without padding: - instead of +, no =. The hex form of the same digest is not what PKCE uses.

questions.q: How long is a verifier made from 32 random bytes? What does this print?
questions.explain: 32 bytes are 256 bits; base64 uses 6 bits per character, so 43 characters (the 44th would be padding, which is removed). That is exactly the minimum length PKCE allows.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: URLSearchParams percent-encodes reserved characters and writes spaces as +. Building URLs this way, not by string concatenation, keeps values such as the redirect URI from breaking the query.

questions.q: The client parses a callback. What does this print?
questions.explain: The state matches, so this callback belongs to our log-in, and it reports that Ada declined. Checking the state first means a forged callback cannot even make the app display an attacker's error.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Exact string matching accepts only the registered URI, byte for byte. A trailing slash, different case or extra query all fail; clients simply send exactly what they registered.

questions.q: An ID token's claims are checked. What does this print?
questions.explain: Everything about this token is genuine, except that it was issued to Quiz App. One failed check is enough to reject it; that is the audience check doing its job.
options: { issuer: true, audience: false, notExpired: true, nonce: true } false
{ issuer: true, audience: true, notExpired: true, nonce: true } true
{ issuer: true, audience: false, notExpired: true, nonce: true } true
{ issuer: false, audience: false, notExpired: true, nonce: true } false

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Scopes are checked by exact name. The token was never granted transactions:write, so the transfer is forbidden even though the token itself is valid.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: //evil.example/x starts with a slash but is a protocol-relative URL pointing at another site, so it is refused. Only paths on the app's own origin survive.

questions.q: Write async function pkcePair(bytes) that turns a Uint8Array into a base64url verifier and returns { verifier, challenge }, where the challenge is base64url(SHA-256(verifier)) using crypto.subtle. Print the pair for 32 bytes all equal to 7.
questions.explain: The challenge is the hash of the verifier's text (its ASCII characters), not of the original random bytes. Real code uses crypto.getRandomValues for the bytes; fixed bytes here make the output checkable.

questions.q: Write createPendingLogins() with save(loginId, state) and take(loginId, state). take returns true only when a pending log-in exists for loginId and its state equals the given one; the entry is deleted on every take, whether or not it matches.
questions.explain: Deleting before deciding makes every pending log-in single-use: a failed attempt burns it, and a successful callback cannot be replayed. Real code compares with a constant-time function; the logic is the same.

questions.q: Write async function redeem(codes, form) for a token endpoint. codes maps a code to { clientId, redirectUri, challenge, used }. Return "invalid_grant" for an unknown code, a different client or redirect URI, a used code, or a verifier whose base64url SHA-256 does not equal the challenge; otherwise mark it used and return "tokens".
questions.explain: The thief's wrong verifier and the changed redirect URI both fail without using the code up, so the real client can still redeem it once. The second redemption fails because the code is single-use.

questions.q: Write checkIdToken(claims, { issuer, clientId, nonce, now }) (signature already verified) that returns the first failure, in this order: "issuer", "audience", "expired" (exp missing or not after now), "nonce"; or "ok". Times are in seconds.
questions.explain: Four checks, four attacks: a token from another provider, a token meant for another app, an old token, and a token from another log-in. Only a token that passes all of them identifies the user for this log-in.

questions.q: Write guard(tokens, authorization, requiredScope) for a resource server. tokens maps an access token to { scopes, expiresAt }. Return { status: 401, error: "invalid_token" } for a missing, unknown or expired token (expiresAt <= now, with now = 1000), { status: 403, error: "insufficient_scope" } when the scope is missing, else { status: 200 }.
questions.explain: Expiry is checked before scope, so an expired token with every scope still gets 401 and the client knows to get a new token. 403 means "valid token, but not allowed to do this".

questions.q: Write checkAuthorize(params, clients) for an authorization endpoint. Return "error page" if the client is unknown or redirect_uri is not exactly registered; "redirect error=invalid_request" if code_challenge_method is not S256; "redirect error=invalid_scope" if any requested scope is not allowed; otherwise "redirect code".
questions.explain: The client and redirect URI are checked first, because only a verified redirect URI may receive a redirect at all. Every later error is reported back to the client through that verified URI.
questions.expected:
redirect code
error page
redirect error=invalid_request
redirect error=invalid_scope
error page

questions.q: The bank publishes its JWKS at a public URL. Why is that safe?
questions.explain: With RS256, the private key signs and stays with the bank; the public key (modulus n, exponent e) only verifies. Publishing it is the whole point: any client can check the bank's tokens.
options: A JWKS contains only public keys; they can verify signatures but not create them
The keys in it are encrypted
Only registered clients can download it

questions.q: Why do providers sign ID tokens with RS256 (a public/private key pair) rather than HS256 (a shared secret)?
questions.explain: A shared secret gives signing power to everyone who verifies. With thousands of client apps, the provider must be the only party able to sign, which requires an asymmetric key.
options: With HS256, every client that can verify tokens could also forge them; with RS256, clients verify with a public key and only the provider can sign
RS256 does not need an expiry

questions.q: A client picks the verification key by kid. What does this print?
questions.explain: During rotation the set holds both old and new keys. A kid that is not there yet may be a brand-new key, so the client refreshes its copy once; if it is still unknown, the token is rejected. Falling back to "any key" would defeat the check.
options:
bank-key-2026-09
unknown key: refetch the JWKS once, then reject

bank-key-2026-08
unknown key: refetch the JWKS once, then reject

questions.q: An authorization code is valid for 60 seconds and single-use. What does this print?
questions.explain: The first redemption succeeds and uses the code up; every later one fails, whether it comes 10 seconds or 80 seconds later. A short lifetime limits how long a leaked code is even worth trying.

questions.q: Write buildAuthorizeUrl(base, { clientId, redirectUri, scopes, state, nonce, challenge }) that returns the full authorization URL with response_type=code, the given values, scope joined with spaces and code_challenge_method=S256, built with URL and URLSearchParams. Print the URL's parameter names and the decoded scope and redirect_uri.
questions.explain: Everything in this URL is visible to the browser and anyone watching it, which is why it holds a challenge instead of the verifier and a client id instead of the secret. URLSearchParams handles the encoding, so the values arrive intact.
